images.title: File:Top view of the famed Lycurgus Cup in the British Museum, showing the glass both green and ruby red.jpg
images.description: Top view of the Lycurgus Cup, a 4th c. CE ‘cage cup’, demonstrating how direct light onto the surface of its dichroic glass makes it appear jade green, but backlighting makes it glow a ruby red. This was achieved by the ancient glassmakers adding nanoparticles of gold and silver to the glass, a technique we’ve only recently come to understand. British Museum (1958,1202.1)
categories: Files with coordinates missing SDC location of creation (51° N, 1° W)

images.title: File:Photo of the 4th c. CE Lycurgus Cup, side view with satyr, British Museum (1958,1202.1).jpg
images.description: Side view of the Lycurgus Cup, the most magnificent of all Roman ‘cage cups’, where the glass is carved away to create almost free-standing relief characters. It’s made of dichroic glass, with nanoparticles of gold and silver, which means that in normal light, the glass appears milky green, and when backlit, it glows a ruby red. Here, we see one of Dionysus’ satyrs about to hurt a stone at King Ly

images.title: File:British Museum The Lycurgus Cup 03 15022019 4320.jpg
images.description:
The Lycurgus Cup, a cage-cup ( diatreta ) made of dichroic glass, Late Roman Empire, 300s AD. Gilded silver rim and foot were probably added in the late 1700s.
Information provided by the British Museum : "its glass contains tiny amount of gold and silver which cause it to turn from opaque green to translucent red when light is shone through."
Room 41, British Museum.
categories: Taken with Canon EOS-1D Mark IV
